sentences.text: The name Goyocephale translates to decorated head, merging a Mongolian term for ornamentation with a Greek word for the cranium.
The specific epithet lattimorei commemorates the explorer Owen Lattimore.
Small bony bumps along the back edge of the skull roof suggest the animal grew small horns.
Its teeth were varied in shape, including large canine-like front teeth and regular triangular ones further back.
The upper arm bone is noticeably curved, showing similar widening at both ends.
This creature likely weighed between 10 and 40 kilograms and reached a length of about 2 meters.
The skull features elongated oval openings on the top with a narrow strip of bone connecting them.
A distinctive trait is the wavy outer edge of the skull, which is especially noticeable above the eye socket.
The genus was first named in 1982 by Altangerel Perle, Teresa Maryańska, and Halszka Osmólska.
They described the species based on a broken skull, jaws, and scattered body parts found in Mongolia.
Goyocephale inhabited Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous period roughly 76 million years ago.
Its existence spanned the Santonian through Maastrichtian stages, from 85.7 to 66 million years ago.
This animal belongs to the dinosaur group Pachycephalosauria.
It is classified within the ornithischian dinosaur class.
Originally, it was placed in the family Homalocephalidae alongside the genus Homalocephale.
Modern studies often view Homalocephalidae as a paraphyletic group, positioning Goyocephale as a sister branch to Pachycephalosauridae.
However, one analysis supports a single Homalocephalidae family, listing Goyocephale, Homalocephale, and Wannanosaurus as the most advanced members.
It is also described as a primitive pachycephalosaurid originally assigned to Homalocephalidae.
Many recent analyses suggest Homalocephalidae is paraphyletic, with its genera acting as early branches within Pachycephalosauridae leading to Prenocephale.
Another study identified Goyocephale, Homalocephale, and Wannanosaurus as the most derived pachycephalosaurids within a monophyletic Homalocephalidae.
Scientists propose that the advanced position of Asian pachycephalosaurians like Goyocephale implies the group originated in North America before moving to Asia.
The fact that Asian species appear most derived suggests pachycephalosaurids may have evolved in North America, where they kept their highest diversity, prior to migration to Asia.
